interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a square of pinned bars folding flat while a triangle keeps its shape, until one diagonal bar locks the square, when you drag a joint.
interactive.title: The frame on two supports
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on a frame of bars. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each bar is a straight line between two joints, and each joint is a ring you can drag. The joints are pins, free to turn like hinges. The frame stands on two supports. A pin support under the left foot can push any way. A roller under the right foot can only push straight up. A counter reads the frame's bars against 2j − 3, where j is the number of joints. A load can hang from any joint, and the supports' pushes then appear as arrows with their sizes. Tap a joint, and its forces are drawn nose to tail beside the frame. Each bar's arrow at that pin is labelled pull or push. Here is the rule the picture follows. A bar fixes the distance between its two pins and nothing else. On a flat page each joint can move two ways, across and up, so j joints have 2j ways to move. Three of them, two slides and a turn, move the whole frame without changing its shape, and the supports stop those. Each bar stops one of the rest. So a frame keeps its shape when its bars, placed where each locks something, number at least 2j − 3. Short of that, it has a way left to move, and the drag folds it. Under a load, every joint is in balance. So the forces at a joint, drawn nose to tail, close into a triangle, or a longer shape where more bars meet. Each bar pushes or pulls only along its own length. If its arrow at a pin points away from the pin, the bar pulls, in tension. If it points into the pin, the bar pushes, in compression. The supports' pushes come from moments about one support for the whole frame, as for a mobile's bar. A readout that would give a puzzle's answer shows "?" until the answer is checked. Any row of readouts wraps onto two lines on a phone. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, Which holds?: a square frame and a triangle frame of pinned bars side by side, each standing on a pin support and a roller, with a hand arrow pushing sideways at the top of each. "Push sideways on the top of each frame. Which one keeps its shape?" Choices, in a column: The triangle (right); The square; Both keep their shape; Neither keeps its shape. Hint on The square: "Its four corners are hinges. Nothing stops it leaning over." Hint on Both keep their shape: "Watch the square's corners. They turn freely." Hint on Neither keeps its shape: "Three bars of fixed length fit together only one way." Read: "A square frame and a triangle frame of pinned bars each stand on two supports. Push sideways on the top of each. Which one keeps its shape?" Why: every joint is a pin, free to turn like a hinge. The square's four bars can lean over together into a diamond, so it folds. Three bars of fixed length make one triangle and no other, so the triangle cannot change shape. After Check both frames are pushed. The square folds flat and the triangle holds. Screen 2, show, Triangles hold: both frames again, the square folded over. Words: "A pin lets bars turn at a joint, like a hinge. So a bar fixes only the distance between its two pins. Three fixed lengths make one triangle and no other, so a triangle of pinned bars is rigid. Four fixed lengths make a square or a thin diamond, so a square folds." Then "Drag any joint." Read: "Dragged by one joint, the square leans over until it folds flat. The triangle's joints will not move." Screen 3, show, Counting ways to move: the triangle and the square, with a counter under each reading its bars against 2j − 3. Words: "On a flat page, each joint can move two ways, across and up. Three of those ways slide or turn the whole frame without changing its shape. Each bar stops one of the rest. So a frame of j joints needs at least 2j − 3 bars to hold its shape." Then "Tap the triangle, then the square." Read: "The triangle has 3 joints and 3 bars, and 2 × 3 − 3 = 3, so it holds. The square has 4 joints and 4 bars, one short of 2 × 4 − 3 = 5, so it folds." Screen 4, do, typed, Lock the square: the square frame on its two supports, its counter showing "?". "A square frame has 4 joints. What is the fewest bars it needs to hold its shape?" A typed answer: 5 bars, a whole number. Slips: 4 bars, "That is what the square has now, and it folds."; 8 bars, "That counts all 2 × 4 ways to move. Three of them only slide or turn the whole frame."; 6 bars, "That joins every pair of joints. One of those bars is spare." Hint: "Use 2j − 3, with j the number of joints." Why: 2 × 4 − 3 = 5 bars. The square has 4, so one way to move is left, and it folds. A diagonal is the fifth bar. It splits the square into two triangles. After Check the diagonal appears, and dragging a joint no longer moves it. The counter shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 5, do, typed, Grow the frame: two square bays side by side on the supports, with a diagonal in the left bay only, the right bay leaning. "This frame has 6 joints and 8 bars. How many more bars does it need to hold its shape?" A typed answer: 1 bar, a whole number. Slips: 4 bars, "2 × 6 − 8 leaves out the three ways that only slide or turn the whole frame."; 9 bars, "9 is the total it needs. It already has 8."; 0 bars, "The right bay still leans over. Count again against 2j − 3." Hint: "Find 2j − 3, then take away the 8 bars it has." Read: "A frame of two square bays has 6 joints and 8 bars. How many more bars does it need to hold its shape?" Why: 2 × 6 − 3 = 9 bars. It has 8, so it needs 1 more, a diagonal across the right bay. Each new joint brings two ways to move, so it needs two new bars. That is why a frame grown one triangle at a time keeps the count right. After Check the second diagonal appears and the right bay locks. Screen 6, show, The supports push back: the triangle frame, its sloping bars at 30° to level, the pin support under its left foot and the roller under its right foot. Words: "Hang a load on a joint, and the supports push back. Find those pushes first. Treat the whole frame as one body and take moments about one support, as for a mobile's bar. The pin can push any way, but the roller only straight up." Then "Hang the load on a joint." Read: "A 10 kN load hangs from the top joint, midway between the supports. Each support pushes up with 5 kN." Screen 7, do, typed, Off centre: a longer frame of five triangles on the supports, 6 m between them, with 4 joints along the bottom 2 m apart and 3 along the top. A 12 kN load hangs from the bottom joint 2 m from the left support. The reaction arrows show "?". "A frame spans 6 m between its supports. A 12 kN load hangs from a joint 2 m from the left support. How hard does the left support push up?" A typed answer: 8 kN, a whole number. Slips: 4 kN, "That is the right support's share. The support nearer the load carries more."; 6 kN, "Half each is right only for a load in the middle." Hint: "Take moments about the right support." Read: "A frame spans 6 m between its supports. A 12 kN load hangs from a joint 2 m from the left support. How hard does the left support push up?" Why: the load is 6 − 2 = 4 m from the right support. Its moment about that support is 12 × 4 = 48 kN m. The left support's push, 6 m away, must balance it, so it is 48 ÷ 6 = 8 kN. The right support takes the rest, 12 − 8 = 4 kN. The reactions show "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 8, show, Pull or push: one bar between two pins, with an arrow at each pin. Words: "Each bar in a loaded frame is pulled or pushed along its length. Look at its arrow at a pin. If it points away from the pin, the bar pulls, and it is in tension. If it points into the pin, the bar pushes, and it is in compression." Then "Drag one pin to stretch or squash the bar." Read: "A stretched bar pulls its pins towards each other, so its arrow at each pin points away from that pin, labelled pull. A squashed bar pushes its pins apart, so each arrow points into its pin, labelled push." Screen 9, do, Which is pulled?: the triangle frame from screen 6 with its 10 kN load at the top joint, the bar arrows hidden. "A triangle frame carries a load at its top joint. Which bar is in tension?" Choices, in a column: The bottom bar (right); The two sloping bars; All three bars; None of them. Hint on The two sloping bars: "The load presses them down onto the supports. They are squashed." Hint on All three bars: "The load squashes the sloping bars. Only one bar is stretched." Hint on None of them: "Something must stop the two feet sliding apart." Read: "A triangle frame carries a load at its top joint. Which bar is in tension?" Why: the load presses the top joint down and squashes both sloping bars. Squashed, they push their feet outwards. The roller cannot push sideways, so the bottom bar holds the feet together, by pulling. After Check, every bar's arrows and its pull or push label appear. Screen 10, show, Joint by joint: the same frame and load, with the top joint's three forces drawn nose to tail beside it. Words: "At each joint the forces balance, so drawn nose to tail they close into a triangle. Start at a joint with only two unknown bars, such as the top joint. The two bars slope equally, so each one's up part holds half the load, 5 kN. That up part is the bar's force × sin 30°, so each bar pushes with 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 kN." Then "Tap the top joint." Read: "At the top joint, the 10 kN load and the two sloping bars' 10 kN pushes close into a triangle with three equal sides. Both arrows point into the pin, so both sloping bars are in compression." Screen 11, do, typed, The bottom bar: the left foot of the same frame, with the support's 5 kN push up, the sloping bar's 10 kN push into the foot, and the bottom bar's force showing "?". "At the left foot, the support pushes up with 5 kN. The sloping bar pushes into the foot with 10 kN, at 30° above level. What is the force in the bottom bar?" A typed answer: 8.66 kN, to two decimal places. Slips: 10 kN, "That is the sloping bar's whole force. The bottom bar balances only its across part."; 5 kN, "That is the up part, 10 × sin 30°. Use the across part."; 11.55 kN, "Multiply by cos 30°, rather than divide." Hint: "Balance the across parts at the foot." Read: "At the left foot, the support pushes up with 5 kN. The sloping bar pushes into the foot with 10 kN, at 30° above level. What is the force in the bottom bar?" Why: the sloping bar's across part is 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 kN, pushing the foot outwards. Its up part, 10 × sin 30° = 5 kN, matches the support's push. So the bottom bar must pull the foot inwards with 8.66 kN. Its arrow points away from the pin, so it is in tension. The force shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 12, show, A screw is a ramp: a screw whose thread unrolls, one turn at a time, into a ramp. Words: "A screw's thread is a ramp wrapped round a shaft. One turn of thread, unrolled, runs as far as the screw's circumference and climbs one pitch, the gap between threads. With friction ignored, the work in equals the work out. So the load lifted is bigger than the push by the ramp's length ÷ its climb." Then "Play the unrolling." Read: "One turn of a 20 mm screw's thread unrolls into a ramp 62.8 mm long that climbs 2 mm. With friction ignored, a push along the thread lifts 31.4 times its size." Still: the thread fully unrolled. Screen 13, do, mixed, Same count: two frames of two square bays each. Frame A has a diagonal in each bay. Frame B has both diagonals crossed in its left bay and none in its right. "Both frames have 6 joints and 9 bars, as 2j − 3 asks. Which one folds?" Choices, in a column: Frame B, both diagonals in one bay (right); Frame A, a diagonal in each bay; Neither, since both have 9 bars; Both of them. Hint on Frame A: "Each of its bays is two triangles. Nothing in it can lean." Hint on Neither: "The count says how many bars, not where. Look at Frame B's right bay." Hint on Both of them: "Frame A's two bays are both split into triangles." Read: "Two frames of two square bays each have 6 joints and 9 bars. Frame A has a diagonal in each bay. Frame B has both diagonals in its left bay. Which one folds?" Why: the count says how many bars a frame needs, not where they go. Frame B's second diagonal locks nothing the first had not, so it is spare. Its right bay is a square with no diagonal, so it folds. After Check, Frame B's right bay leans over. Screen 14, do, mixed, typed, A steeper frame: a triangle frame on the two supports, its sloping bars at 45° to level, a 12 kN load at its top joint, each sloping bar's force showing "?". "A triangle frame on two supports carries 12 kN at its top joint. Its sloping bars are at 45° to level. What force is in each sloping bar?" A typed answer: 8.49 kN, to two decimal places. Slips: 6 kN, "That is each bar's up part. The bar slopes, so its force is bigger."; 12 kN, "The two sloping bars share the load."; 4.24 kN, "Divide the up part by sin 45°, rather than multiply." Hint: "Each sloping bar's up part holds half the load." Read: "A triangle frame on two supports carries 12 kN at its top joint. Its sloping bars are at 45° to level. What force is in each sloping bar?" Why: the two bars slope equally, so they share the load equally. Each up part is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kN. The up part is the force × sin 45°, so the force is 6 ÷ 0.707 = 8.49 kN. Both arrows point into the top joint, so both bars are in compression. At each foot the bottom bar then pulls with 8.49 × cos 45° = 6.00 kN. The forces show "?" until the answer is checked.
interactive.ignores: The bars are drawn weightless, and every load hangs at a joint. The pins turn with no friction. Real frames are bolted or welded, so their joints resist turning a little, and their bars bend a little as well as stretching or squashing. The bars stretch and squash too little to see, so the picture keeps their lengths fixed. Nothing here breaks. A long, thin bar in compression can bow sideways and fail well below the force that would crush it, and the picture does not show that. Everything is drawn flat. A real frame also needs bracing across its width. The screw is a single thread, so one turn moves it one pitch, and its friction is left out. Real screws lose a good part of the push to friction. Every load, length and angle is an example figure, not a real frame's.

explain.text:
A frame of bars joined by pins holds its shape when it is built from triangles. Put a load on it, and each bar is either pulled or pushed along its length. Balancing the forces at each joint in turn tells you which, and how hard.

Start with why triangles hold. A pin lets the bars turn at a joint, like a hinge. So a bar fixes only one thing, the distance between its two pins. Three fixed lengths make one triangle and no other, so a triangle of three pinned bars is rigid.[^1] Four fixed lengths can make a square or a thin diamond, so a square folds. You can count this. On a flat page each joint can move two ways, across and up, so j joints have 2j ways to move. Three of those ways, two slides and a turn, move the whole frame without changing its shape, and the supports stop those. Each of the other ways changes the shape, and each bar stops one. Each way left to move is a [[degree of freedom]], and a frame with one left can fold. So a frame needs at least 2j − 3 bars to hold its shape. A simple frame, grown one triangle at a time, has exactly m = 2j − 3, where m is the number of bars.[^2] A square has 4 joints, so it needs 5 bars. With only 4 it has a degree of freedom left, and a diagonal as the fifth bar locks it. The count tells you how many bars, not where they go. Each one must lock something, as a diagonal does when it splits a square into two triangles.

Now the forces. First find the supports' pushes, treating the whole frame as one body. Total clockwise moment about one support equals total anticlockwise moment about it, just as on a mobile's bar.[^4] Then go joint by joint. The count says why that works for a simple frame. Its j joints give 2j balance equations, two each, and its m bars and three support pushes are m + 3 = 2j unknowns. Each joint is in balance, so its forces drawn nose to tail close into a triangle. Start at a joint with only two unknown bars. Take a triangle frame on two supports, its sloping bars at 30° to level, with 10 kN hung from the top joint. Each support pushes up 5 kN. At the top joint, the two sloping bars slope equally, so each one's up part holds half the load, 5 kN. That up part is the bar's force × sin 30°, so each bar carries 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10 kN. At a foot, the same bar's across part is 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 kN, pushing the foot outwards. The roller cannot push sideways, so the bottom bar must pull the feet together, with 8.66 kN. To tell a pull from a push, look at the bar's arrow at the pin. Pointing away from the pin, the bar is in [[tension]]. Pointing into the pin, it is in [[compression]].[^3] Here the sloping bars push and the bottom bar pulls.

Weightless bars, frictionless pins and loads only at joints make this a teaching model. Real joints are bolted or welded, and real bars bend a little as well. **A frame of pinned bars built from triangles holds its shape, and balancing the forces joint by joint shows which bars are pulled and which pushed.**

analogy.text: Working out a frame joint by joint is like working out a circuit's branch currents node by node. At every node, the currents in equal the currents out. At every joint, the forces balance. Each balance gives an equation, and with enough equations every unknown comes out. Guess a direction for each one. If the answer comes out negative, it runs the other way: for a current, the other way round its branch, and for a bar, a push instead of a pull.
analogy.breaks: A node gives one equation, because a current has only a size and a sense along its wire. A joint gives two, across and up, because a force can point any way on the page. And a circuit has nothing like a frame folding. A missing wire leaves a current with nowhere to flow, not a shape free to move.

practice.text:
- Where a frame carries a real load, such as a lifting beam or a scaffold, keep to its marked safe working load and the site's lifting plan first. These sums explain a frame. They do not make one safe.
- Count the joints and bars. Check the bars against 2j − 3, and look for any four-sided bay with no diagonal.
- Draw the whole frame with its loads. Find the supports' pushes by taking moments about one support.
- Pick a joint with only two unknown bars. Draw its forces nose to tail, or balance the across parts and the up parts separately.
- Solve for the two bar forces.
- Read each bar's arrow at that pin. Away from the pin is tension. Into the pin is compression.
- Move to a joint that now has only two unknowns, and repeat.
- Check the last joint. Its forces should balance with nothing left over.

**Rule of thumb:** a four-sided bay with no diagonal will lean over under a sideways push. In a simple triangle frame loaded at its top, the sloping bars push and the bottom bar pulls. The flatter the sloping bars, the harder they work.

**Worked example:** a triangle frame on two supports carries 20 kN at its top joint, with its sloping bars at 60° to level. Each support pushes up 20 ÷ 2 = 10 kN. At the top joint, each sloping bar's up part holds 10 kN, so its force is 10 ÷ sin 60° = 10 ÷ 0.866 = 11.55 kN. Its arrow points into the top joint, so it is in compression. At a foot, its across part is 11.55 × cos 60° = 11.55 × 0.5 = 5.77 kN. So the bottom bar pulls with 5.77 kN, in tension.

**Common mistakes**
- Counting 2j bars and forgetting the three the supports take away.
- Trusting the count alone. A spare bar in one bay cannot lock another.
- Starting at a joint with three unknown bars, or before the supports' pushes are known.
- Using cos where the up part needs sin, or multiplying when the bar's force needs a divide.
- Reading pull or push from where an arrow sits on the drawing, rather than from which way it points at the pin.
- Letting a roller push sideways. On level ground it only pushes straight up.

sources.title: Chapter 6 ANALYSIS OF STRUCTURES
sources.quote: A truss is said to be rigid if it is designed in such a way that it will not greatly deform or collapse under a small load. A triangular truss consisting of three members connected at three joints is clearly a rigid truss.

sources.title: Trusses
sources.quote: In a simple truss, m = 2j - 3 # where m is the total number of members and j is the number of joints.

sources.title: Chapter 6 ANALYSIS OF STRUCTURES
sources.quote: If the force exerted by a member on a pin is directed toward that pin, the member is in compression ; if it is directed away from the pin, the member is in tension
